hero.headline.text: Decide what you are comparing first

hero.highlight.text: Paired experiments on prompts and tool descriptions: same task, same model

hero.takeaway.text: Same task, same model, same settings. Change one piece of text, then compare the two real responses by the same rule. One result counts as one observation.

concepts.01-goal.title.text: Change one thing at a time

concepts.01-goal.description.text: A controlled experiment changes one condition at a time: the task, the model, and the sampling temperature stay fixed. Two of the tool description presets change only the tool description. The other two change only a rule in the system prompt.

concepts.02-check.title.text: A tool description is a decision input

concepts.02-check.description.text: The model reads the description to decide whether to call and how to fill the arguments. "Tool description: vague vs. clear" only records the tool call proposal and does not execute it. "Tool description matrix" executes the proposal so you can see what the code really returns.

concepts.03-evidence.description.text: A keyword screen cannot prove a whole sentence is correct. Whether it hits or misses, go back to the raw response and review it by hand.

concepts.04-matrix.title.text: The description must match the code

concepts.04-matrix.description.text: The description says the tool concatenates, but the code adds. The model decides by the description, yet what runs is the code.

section-1.title.text: Decide what you are comparing first

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Whether a prompt change is good has to be judged by a controlled experiment, not by reading one answer and feeling it looks better. Say you change the system prompt from "Give the answer." to a rule that spells out steps, and run it again, and the answer is indeed more complete. But this time you also switched models, and moved the temperature from 0 to 0.7. Which change made the answer better? You cannot tell. {{lesson:sampling-variance}} also showed that sending the exact same request again can give a different answer.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson works in pairs: same task, same model, same call budget, temperature set to 0 for both, one piece of text changed, and each version requested once. The version you did not change is the baseline, and the changed one is the variant. The first three presets are all pairs of requests like this: "Tool description: vague vs. clear" changes only function.description, while "Process rule: answer and check" and "Failure boundary: missing addend" change only a rule in the system prompt. The fourth preset, "Tool description matrix", expands a pair into six cells and is covered separately below.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: Before comparing, write down the judging rule, and judge both versions by the same rule. The rule lives in Python: for tool scenarios it looks at the name and arguments of the tool call proposal, and for text scenarios it checks whether certain wording appears in the answer. {{lesson:task-contract}} wrote "what counts as done" into the task card in advance, and {{lesson:structured-output}} had the program check the model's output layer by layer. This is the same idea: set the standard first, then look at the result, instead of looking at the result and then hunting for reasons.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: Two limits remain. temperature=0 does not guarantee that two requests are reproducible, so a pair of results may include sampling noise. Each version also ran only once, so it counts as a single observation. That is why this lesson's report says only "this time it hit or missed", and never "the variant is better".

section-2.title.text: A tool description is a decision input

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: When the model decides whether to call a tool and how to fill its arguments, all it can read about that tool is the tool definition in the request. It cannot see the Python code. However clearly add_numbers is implemented, the model cannot read it. What it can read is three things in tools: the function name name, the parameter structure parameters, and the usage note description. Of these, description is the tool description written in natural language, and it looks most like a prompt.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: "Tool description: vague vs. clear" fixes the first two and changes only description. The baseline is just "Calculation tool.": it does not say what it calculates, what the two parameters are, or when not to use it. The rewrite reads "Adds two given integers; a is the first addend, b is the second addend. Do not call it if either addend is missing." It states the job, the meaning of the parameters, and when not to call, in that order. The system prompt is the same sentence both times: "Choose a tool or answer according to the user's task."

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: How does the program judge? evaluate_tool_response requires exactly one tool call proposal in the response, with the name add_numbers and arguments that parse to exactly `{"a": 19, "b": 23}`. If the model proposes no call and writes "19 + 23 = 42" directly, that version counts as a miss, and the text is kept in the report unchanged. This step looks only at the proposal and does not execute it.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: A good description only makes the model more likely to propose the right call. It grants no permission to execute anything. Which functions can run is still decided by the allowlist registered in Python. In {{lesson:fail-safely}}, unregistered names and bad arguments were both stopped before execution.

predict-executed-tools.prompt.text: Before running the experiment "Change only the tool description", predict: how many tool_call events will this run produce, that is, how many times does the runner actually execute a tool?

mq-proposal-only.proposal-not-executed.p.text: In the "Tool description: vague vs. clear" preset, the variant's response proposes add_numbers(19, 23). What does the runner do next?

mq-proposal-only.proposal-not-executed.a.text: Only records the proposal and does the structural screen; it does not execute the tool
Correct. This experiment observes the proposal. What can be called is still decided by the Python allowlist.

mq-proposal-only.proposal-not-executed.b.text: Executes add_numbers and sends 42 back to the model
Not quite. This preset does not execute proposals, and no tool_result is sent back.

mq-proposal-only.proposal-not-executed.c.text: Tells the user the proposal directly as the answer
Not quite. The proposal only goes into the report for comparison.

mq-proposal-only.proposal-not-executed.e.text: Proposing a call and executing a call are two different things. Only the first is compared here.

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: A rule written into the system prompt has to show up somewhere visible in the answer before a program can judge it. The task in "Process rule: answer and check" is "The user asks for 19 plus 23; the answer should give the number and say what it is based on." The baseline system prompt is just "Give the answer." The rewrite reads "First identify the two numbers in the input, then compute and check the arithmetic, then give the number and its basis in one sentence."

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: The rewrite is a procedure, not a pile of scattered requirements: what to do first, what next, what to hand in at the end. People reading a scattered list of rules often cannot tell the order or the weight, and the model is the same. In a set of prompt ablations, *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* (深入理解 AI Agent) broke the same rules into unordered items. The book records the task success rate dropping by more than 30%, with the agent often violating key business rules (this is the book's experimental result; this lesson did not reproduce it). When the procedure is clear, the shape of the answer is also more predictable, and the program has something to check.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: What the program checks is a keyword: the answer must contain a standalone number 42, with no other digit right before or after it, and no negation such as "not 42" or "isn't 42". A hit only means 42 appears literally. It cannot prove the whole arithmetic sentence is right, and it cannot show that the model really went through identify, compute, and check in that order. The answer text is only output, and you cannot infer the model's internal process from it.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: The official Claude Code documentation makes the same point when it teaches how to write the project instruction file `CLAUDE.md`: rules should be specific enough to verify. Write "run `npm test` before committing", not "test your changes". When two rules contradict each other, the model may pick either one to follow. The documentation also says `CLAUDE.md` is context handed to the model, not configuration that is enforced, so how you write it affects how reliably the model follows it. This agrees with this lesson's conclusion: putting a rule in the prompt only makes the model more likely to follow it. Whether it did is something you check in the answer.

section-4.title.text: Do not make up missing arguments

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: When information is missing, the right action is to ask, not to fill in a number for the user. In "Failure boundary: missing addend", the task is "The user only says: help me with an addition, but gives no numbers." Here the model can easily make up two numbers and compute them for you. The answer is complete and confident, but it is a guess. Inside an agent it is more dangerous: the invented numbers get treated as real input and passed to the next tool.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: The baseline system prompt is "Handle the user's request." and the rewrite is "If any addend is missing, do not guess; only ask for the missing number." It writes one failure case and the matching action as a rule, which tells the model "when you meet this situation, do this". Tool descriptions can carry this kind of sentence too: "Do not call it if either addend is missing" in the rewritten description is this tool's failure boundary.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: The screening checks three things at once: does it look like a question (a question mark, or "please provide" or "please tell"); does it mention an addend, a number, or the input; and does the whole text contain no digits at all. A hit requires all three. "Compute 1+1=2" contains digits and is stopped. But "Please provide two numbers, such as 3 and 5." also contains digits and is stopped too, even though it really is asking. The simpler the rule, the easier it is to review and the easier it is to misjudge, so you must read the original text.

deep-dive-screening.title.text: Judged by program, by hand, or by model

deep-dive-screening.summary.text: There are roughly three ways to judge model output, each with its own cost and blind spots. This lesson uses only the cheapest and easiest to review, and then hands you the original text.

deep-dive-screening.paragraphs.0.text: There are roughly three ways to judge whether an answer is acceptable. Program: use string comparison, a regular expression, or a structure check, like this lesson's check for "42" and the question mark. Human: a person reads the original text and decides against a standard. Model: ask a judge model (LLM-as-a-Judge) to read the answer and score it. The Claude Cookbooks make the same split when discussing how to build a test set, and advise designing questions so that a program can judge them wherever possible.

deep-dive-screening.paragraphs.1.text: Program judging is cheap and deterministic: judge the same answer a hundred times and you get the same result every time, and the rule itself can be audited line by line. The cost is that it only recognizes the literal text. This lesson's process-rule screening can be fooled by two kinds of answers. "The answer is forty-two" has no digits 42, so it is missed. "I'm not sure, it may be 42 or it may be 43" contains 42 and no negation of 42, so it is wrongly counted as a hit.

deep-dive-screening.paragraphs.2.text: Human judging applies most widely and can judge almost any task, but it is expensive, and every rerun has to be read again. Model judging looks like the best of both, but it adds a new variable: the judge model fluctuates and has preferences of its own, and its judgments should be compared against human conclusions before you trust them. This is why the design trade-offs at the end of the Code scene did not choose "have another model score the two versions".

deep-dive-screening.paragraphs.3.text: So this lesson combines them: the program does a first screen that only answers "does it look right", and the report keeps both original texts for you to make the final call. Whether the screen hits or misses, it is only a clue for when you read the original text.

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.prompt.text: In the variant's answer for "Process rule: answer and check", 42 appears and the screen hits. What can you conclude?

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.a.text.text: The keyword hit this time; you still need to read the original text and repeat the experiment

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.a.feedback.text: Correct. A hit is only a clue.

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.b.text.text: The rewritten prompt is better in general

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.b.feedback.text: Not quite. One pair cannot support a general claim about which is better.

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.c.text.text: The model reasoned internally through the specified steps

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.c.feedback.text: Not quite. You cannot infer the model's internal process from its output text.

mq-keyword-hit.keyword-hit.explanation.text: The screen is a quick filter. Conclusions need review of the original text and repeated runs.

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: The report keeps the original text of both versions and the screening result side by side, and it writes down honestly when the variant got worse. When people change a prompt, they tend to stare at the one problem they wanted to fix, and stop once it is fixed, without noticing that something else got worse. A case of "got worse after the change" is called a regression.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: A pair of results has four combinations. Both versions hit: both passed the screen on this task, and you cannot tell which is better. Baseline misses, variant hits: a clue of improvement. Baseline hits, variant misses: a clue of regression. Read the variant's original text first to see whether it is a side effect of the new rule or a screening error. Both miss: possibly both versions are bad, or possibly the screening rule is too strict.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: In every combination, it is still just one observation. Here is a made-up example: run 5 times before and after the change and get 3 hits and 4 hits. A difference of 1 means little. If you run several batches and the variant hits 5 out of 5 every time while the baseline never goes above 3, that difference is more believable. To reach a reliable conclusion, repeat each pair a few times, switch to a few other tasks, and keep all the original texts. The learner note is written into the report only. It does not change the fixed task.

section-matrix.title.text: Blank, good, misleading: a matrix of three descriptions

section-matrix.paragraphs.0.text: The tool description matrix compares three descriptions at once, to see how the description affects whether and how the model calls. For the same add_numbers, description comes in three kinds: none; clear about the job and its boundaries; and written to say it concatenates two integers into a new integer. Each description gets two probes: "What is 19 plus 23?" needs a call, and "Join 19 and 23 in order into a four-digit number." does not. That makes three rows and two columns, six requests, with the system prompt, the probes, and temperature all unchanged.

section-matrix.paragraphs.1.text: Every cell is judged by the same rule. The sum probe must propose exactly add_numbers with arguments 19 and 23. The concatenation probe must produce no call, because this tool cannot concatenate. Calling when it should not, and not calling when it should, both count as not as expected. The sentence "do not call it unless the user asks for a sum" in the good description is written for exactly the concatenation case.

section-matrix.paragraphs.2.text: The misleading description does not match the code. The model can only see the description and decides by it; what runs is the code. So the matrix experiment really executes the add_numbers call the model proposed, and the report shows both what the model proposed and what the code actually returned. If the model follows the misleading description to "concatenate" and passes the integers 19 and 23, it gets 42, not 1923; if the argument types are wrong, the code reports an error, and the error goes into the table. The model proposed this call, so the runner executes it with execute_proposal: the tool_call event is the call the model gave, with the model's call id. The result only goes into the report and is not sent back to the model.

section-matrix.paragraphs.3.text: The blank description row is worth a look too. With no description, the model can only guess the purpose from the function name and parameter names. The name add_numbers already states the purpose, so a blank description does not necessarily go wrong. A tool with a vague name, such as `calc` or `process`, is where the problem shows up.

deep-dive-description-design.title.text: What goes in a tool description

deep-dive-description-design.summary.text: Job, when to use it, parameter meanings, boundaries, and examples. A good description answers "when to use it and when not to", and it must match the code.

deep-dive-description-design.paragraphs..text: On tool descriptions, *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* stresses that a description should tell the model when to use the tool, not only what it can do. "Calculation tool." says only what it can do. The rewrite also says what the two parameters are and not to call it when a number is missing. Every time the model decides whether to call and how to fill the arguments, these sentences are what it reads.

Boundaries often matter more than abilities: what the tool cannot do and what input it does not accept. The book's point is that many calls go wrong not because the model does not know what the tool can do, but because it does not know what the tool cannot do. In the good description, "Addition only; do not call it unless the user asks for a sum" is a boundary. Parameter notes are best given with an example, such as "a is the first addend, for example 19", which is easier to follow than a type alone.

The description must also match the code. The only world the model sees is the description, while what runs is the code. When the two do not match, a decision the model made from the description plays out differently when executed, and the model cannot notice. The misleading description row demonstrates exactly this. So when you change the code, change the description with it, and, as this lesson does, run the proposal through the real code to verify.

The Hugging Face Agents Course shows how to generate a tool description automatically from a function's type annotations and docstring. The benefit is that the description is written next to the code, so they are less likely to say different things. This lesson writes the description by hand so that it can be changed on its own for the controlled comparison.

misconception-description.claim.text: The clearer the tool description, the more certainly the model calls correctly; if the description is right, the execution result is right too.

misconception-description.correction.text: A description only affects which call the model proposes. It does not guarantee the model follows it, and it does not decide the execution result. The model can still skip the call or fill the arguments wrong, so look at the real response. What gets executed and what it returns is decided by the code. When the description and the code disagree, the model's decision and the execution result do not line up. To verify, run the proposal through the real code once and compare the return value.

mq-matrix.misleading-result.prompt.text: In the cell misleading description × concatenation probe, the model proposed add_numbers(19, 23). What value follows "actually returned" in the report?

mq-matrix.misleading-result.a.feedback.text: Correct. The description affects only the model's decision. The execution result is decided by the code.

mq-matrix.misleading-result.b.text.text: 1923, because the description says it concatenates

mq-matrix.misleading-result.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A description does not change a function's implementation.

mq-matrix.misleading-result.c.text.text: It will not execute, because the description and the code disagree

mq-matrix.misleading-result.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The runner does not know the description is wrong. The name is registered and the arguments are valid, so it runs.

mq-matrix.misleading-result.explanation.text: When the description is wrong, the model's decision and the code's behavior do not line up. That is the harm of a misleading description.

section-next.title.text: From changing one text to removing part of the context

section-next.paragraphs.0.text: Change one thing at a time is the rule shared by all experiments in this lesson, and later lessons will use it again and again. What this lesson changed was explanatory text: the rules in the system prompt and the description in the tool definition. They shape how the model understands the task. The facts the model uses in its answer often come from other parts of the request: earlier conversation and tool results.

section-next.paragraphs.1.text: {{lesson:messages-context}} applies the same method to the whole context: it splits one request into parts, takes away one part at a time, and looks at what the answer is missing. "Change only one thing" becomes "leave out only one part", and the report likewise keeps the original text and gives only a screen.

walkthrough.description.text: Explains the structure of the paired experiment step by step. The code is a simplified illustration. The evidence for this run is in the events on the lab bench.

walkthrough.step-1.title.text: Take the task and the two versions

walkthrough.step-1.body.text: Each scenario in pair_tasks in the message catalog is (task, baseline text, rewritten text); the task is identical in both requests.

walkthrough.step-2.title.text: Request once with the baseline text

walkthrough.step-2.body.text: The platform records the request and response as round 1.

walkthrough.step-3.title.text: Swap only that one text and request again

walkthrough.step-3.body.text: All other fields stay the same. Recorded as round 2.

walkthrough.step-4.title.text: Screen both outputs by the same rule

walkthrough.step-4.body.text: Tool description presets check the name and arguments of the tool call proposal. The other presets do a keyword or form screen.

walkthrough.step-4.evidence.text: passed and detail for each item in the report

walkthrough.step-5.title.text: Report the screen, keep the original text

walkthrough.step-5.body.text: Both raw outputs go into the report, and hit or miss, both need manual review.

walkthrough.step-5.evidence.text: The final answer is only a hint; the two responses and the report are the evidence

references.book-ch4-tools.title.text: Tool design: how to write tool descriptions and their boundaries — Understanding AI Agents in Depth (深入理解 AI Agent)

references.hf-tools.title.text: What are tools: the tool description given to the model must be precise (Hugging Face Agents Course)

references.cookbook-building-evals.title.text: Building a test set: program grading, human grading, and model grading (Claude Cookbooks)

references.cc-claude-md-instructions.tit.text: Writing a good CLAUDE.md: rules specific enough to verify (Claude Code documentation)

code-conditions.n5.text.text: Each paired scenario is three pieces of text: user task, baseline, rewrite. Within a scenario the task is fixed; only the last two differ.

code-conditions.n23.text.text: The two versions in the tool description scenario differ in the description: the baseline says only "Calculation tool.", and the rewrite spells out the parameter meanings and when not to call.

code-conditions.n25.text.text: missing_input deliberately gives no numbers, to see whether the rewritten rule makes the model ask instead of making up an answer.

code-conditions.n28.text.text: The system prompt is fixed and the variable lives only in the tool description, so any behavior difference can be attributed to the description.

code-conditions.n32.text.text: The blank group has no entry here: tool_spec receives None and leaves out the description field.

code-conditions.n35.text.text: The misleading description deliberately disagrees with the implementation of add_numbers. The matrix hands the model's proposal to the real code to execute.

code-conditions.n40.text.text: For the concatenation question the expectation is "no call": it checks whether the model uses the tool for something it cannot do.

code-paired-run.n108.text.text: A pair needs at least two calls. If the budget is too small, the run is rejected outright and never half-run.

code-paired-run.n102.text.text: The three pieces of text come from the message catalog in the run's language: task, baseline, rewrite.

code-paired-run.n115.text.text: In the tool description scenario the system prompt is fixed. In the process rule and missing-input scenarios the variable is the system prompt itself.

code-paired-run.n119.text.text: The tool description scenario puts the variable into function.description; tool_spec always uses the same PARAMETERS, so the parameter schema is identical in both requests.

code-paired-run.n121.text.text: The model, user task, and temperature are the same in both requests. The platform records the request and response as they are.

code-paired-run.n123.text.text: Tool scenarios do only a structural screen: do the name and arguments match. They look at the proposal and do not execute this call.

code-paired-run.n126.text.text: Text scenarios do a keyword or form screening and exclude negations such as "not 42". A hit still needs a human review.

code-paired-run.n128.text.text: The original text and the screening conclusion are kept together, and the report summary states that a single pair cannot support a general claim about which is better.

code-matrix.n162.text.text: Each of the six cells needs one request. If the budget is short, the run is rejected before the first request.

code-matrix.n165.text.text: The outer loop is the description group, the inner loop the probe: each row of the table is one description on the two probes.

code-matrix.n157.text.text: The blank group has no description in the message catalog, so this is None.

code-matrix.n171.text.text: The only variable is tool_spec(description). The system prompt, the question, and temperature are the same in all six requests.

code-matrix.n175.text.text: judge_cell looks only at the proposal: the sum question must propose exactly add_numbers(19, 23), and the concatenation question must produce no call.

code-matrix.n178.text.text: Execution happens after judging: the result goes into the table but does not change whether this cell met expectations.

code-matrix.n187.text.text: For a cell with no proposal, the model's text answer is recorded, for example answering 1923 directly on the concatenation question.

code-matrix.n192.text.text: Only a proposal whose name is add_numbers and whose arguments parse to an object is executed. Other proposals are only recorded.

code-matrix.n193.text.text: The model proposed this call, so it goes through execute_proposal: the tool_call event is the call the model gave, with the model's call id, not marked as made by the program. The allowlist holds this one pure function.

code-matrix.n196.text.text: When the proposal follows the misleading description and the arguments are integers, you would expect 1923, but the code returns 42.

code-decision.title.text: Single-variable pairing plus a screen, with no verdict on which is better

code-decision.chosen.text: Same model, same user task, temperature=0, change one piece of text, call once each. Screen by structure or keyword, and keep both raw outputs in the report for manual review.

code-decision.change-many.title.text: Rewrite several parts of the prompt at once

code-decision.change-many.why_not.text: If the output changes, you cannot attribute it to any one change.

code-decision.llm-judge.title.text: Have another model score the two versions

code-decision.llm-judge.why_not.text: It adds a new uncontrolled variable, and the judge model's own bias cannot be verified in this lesson.

code-decision.single-run-verdict.title.text: Declare a winner after one run

code-decision.single-run-verdict.why_not.text: A single sample cannot support a general rule, and this limit is written straight into the report summary.

tool-description.hypothesis.text: With system, user task, model, and temperature unchanged, change only function.description, from "Calculation tool." to a description that states the job and parameter meanings. The model is then more likely to propose an add_numbers call with the correct name and arguments.

tool-description.tool-description.label.text: One request each for the same task: baseline description "Calculation tool." vs. the rewritten description

tool-description.variant-description.tex.text: The variant request's function.description: the only difference between the two requests.

tool-description.same-settings.text.text: The variant request's temperature: the same as the baseline, 0.

tool-description.baseline-reply.text.text: The baseline response: does the model answer directly or propose a call?

tool-description.variant-proposal.text.text: The tool call proposal in the variant response: tool name and arguments.

tool-description.screening.text.text: The report's two screening items: they check only the call name and arguments. This is not a semantic acceptance check.

tool-description.guide.0.text.text: A paired experiment first confirms "only one thing changed". Compare the two requests.

tool-description.guide.1.text.text: The baseline description is just "Calculation tool.".

tool-description.guide.2.text.text: The variant description states the job, the parameter meanings, and not to call when an argument is missing. The system prompt, user task, and model did not change.

tool-description.guide.3.text.text: The sampling temperature is the same. temperature=0 reduces variation but does not guarantee full reproducibility.

tool-description.guide.4.text.text: Look at the baseline's response this time: did the model give text directly, or propose a call?

tool-description.guide.5.text.text: If the variant proposed a call, the tool name and arguments are here. Note: this is only a proposal, and this experiment does not execute it.

tool-description.guide.6.text.text: The screen compares only the name and arguments. A hit is not a semantic acceptance check, and a miss still means you should go back to the original text.

tool-description.conclusion.proves.0.text: The only difference in this pair of requests is function.description; it also shows what response each version got this time and how the screen came out.

tool-description.conclusion.proves.1.text: Even if the variant proposed a call, the runner did not execute it: this run has no tool_call events.

tool-description.conclusion.does_not_pro.text: One pair cannot prove the variant is better in general. temperature=0 also does not guarantee reproducibility, so you need to repeat the run several times.
A screening hit only shows the name and arguments match. It cannot prove the model understood the tool.
In offline test mode the two responses come from a deterministic script.

system-rule.hypothesis.text: With the user task unchanged and only the rule in system changed, the form of the answer changes with the rule. But a keyword or form screen can only hint at hit or miss. It cannot prove the answer is semantically correct.

system-rule.flow-rule.label.text: Process rule: baseline "Give the answer." vs. a rule stating the steps identify, compute, check

system-rule.missing-input.label.text: Missing-input rule: the user gave no numbers; baseline "Handle the user's request." vs. a rule to only ask for the missing number

system-rule.variant-system.text.text: The variant request's system content: the only change in this pair.

system-rule.same-task.text.text: The variant request's user task: word for word the same as the baseline.

system-rule.baseline-answer.text.text: The baseline answer, in its original text.

system-rule.variant-answer.text.text: The variant answer, in its original text.

system-rule.screening-detail.text.text: The note on the rewrite's screening: even on a hit it says "still needs a human review".

system-rule.guide.0.text.text: This experiment changes only the rule in system. First confirm the scope of the change.

system-rule.guide.1.text.text: The baseline rule is very short.

system-rule.guide.2.text.text: The variant rule is more specific, and this is the only difference between the two requests.

system-rule.guide.3.text.text: The user task is word for word the same, which is what makes the comparison meaningful.

system-rule.guide.4.text.text: Read the baseline answer's original text first.

system-rule.guide.5.text.text: Then read the variant answer's original text: is the difference exactly what the rule asked for?

system-rule.guide.6.text.text: The screening note says it plainly: a hit is only a clue and still needs manual review.

system-rule.conclusion.proves.0.text: The only difference in this pair of requests is the system rule; it also shows the original text of both answers and the screening result this time.

system-rule.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: A keyword hit cannot prove the whole arithmetic sentence or its meaning is correct, and it cannot show whether the model reasoned step by step internally.

system-rule.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: A single pair cannot support a claim about which prompt is better in general. You need to fix more cases and run them repeatedly.

system-rule.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: In offline test mode the answers come from a deterministic script.

tool-matrix.title.text: Tool description matrix: blank, good, misleading

tool-matrix.hypothesis.text: When only description changes, whether the model calls and how it fills the arguments will change with it. When the description and the code disagree, the model's decision and the execution result do not line up.

tool-matrix.blank-function.text.text: The blank row's function definition: only a name and parameters, no description.

tool-matrix.misleading-description.text.text: The misleading row's description: it says concatenate, but the code adds.

tool-matrix.same-system.text.text: The system prompt of request 6: word for word the same across all six requests.

tool-matrix.misleading-proposal.text.text: Misleading row × concatenation question: what call the model proposed (if it did).

tool-matrix.executed-result.text.text: The code's real return value after this proposal was executed.

tool-matrix.matrix-table.text.text: The report's matrix: each cell states what the model did, what the code returned, and whether it met expectations.

tool-matrix.guide.0.text.text: The six requests differ only in the tool description. First see what the model has when there is no description.

tool-matrix.guide.1.text.text: The blank row has only the function name and parameter names. The model has to guess the purpose from the name add_numbers.

tool-matrix.guide.2.text.text: The misleading row's description says it joins two numbers together, which does not match the code.

tool-matrix.guide.3.text.text: The system prompt is word for word the same across the six requests, and the only variable is the description.

tool-matrix.guide.4.text.text: The concatenation question does not need this tool. See whether the model proposes a call under the misleading description.

tool-matrix.guide.5.text.text: If it did, the runner hands the proposal to the real add_numbers to execute. With integer arguments it returns the sum, not the concatenation the description promised. With the wrong type it returns an error.

tool-matrix.guide.6.text.text: Finally, compare the whole matrix. Each cell ran once, so it shows what happened this time, not which description is better in general.

tool-matrix.conclusion.proves.0.text: The six requests differ only in description (the blank row has no such field), and each cell's proposal and execution result are in the events.

tool-matrix.conclusion.proves.1.text: An executed proposal used the real add_numbers. The value after "actually returned" in the table is the code's output, not the description's promise.

tool-matrix.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: Each cell ran once, so this does not show that any description is better in general. A different model, a different question, or another run could change the result.

tool-matrix.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: The name add_numbers itself suggests addition, so part of the blank row's behavior comes from the function name. A tool with a vague name needs separate testing.

tool-matrix.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: In offline test mode the behavior of the six cells comes from a deterministic script.

inputs.scenario.options.tool_matrix.labe.text: Tool description matrix: blank, good, misleading

quiz.q1.prompt.text: If the variant passes in one pair, can you claim it is better than the baseline in general?

quiz.q1.a.text.text: Yes; the variant passing this time means it will do better on all tasks.

quiz.q1.a.feedback.text: A single sample cannot rule out chance. With a different task or another run, the result could be different.

quiz.q1.b.text.text: No; one pair is only one sample, and you need more pairs and manual review.

quiz.q1.b.feedback.text: Correct. This lesson's report also notes that a single pair cannot support a general claim. Keep the full pair records and widen the sample.

quiz.q1.explanation.text: A single sample cannot rule out chance and scenario differences. Keep the full pair records and widen the sample.

quiz.q2.prompt.text: If the two requests used different models, would it still count as changing only the prompt?

quiz.q2.a.text.text: No; a model change is an extra variable, so the difference cannot be attributed to the prompt alone.

quiz.q2.a.feedback.text: Correct. The model is an extra variable. The difference may come from the model or from the prompt, and you cannot attribute it to either alone.

quiz.q2.b.text.text: Yes, as long as both answer the same question.

quiz.q2.b.feedback.text: Answering the same question only fixes the task. The model, sampling settings, and budget must also be fixed for it to be a single-variable comparison.

quiz.q2.explanation.text: A paired experiment must fix the model, user task, sampling settings, and budget. After changing the model, at least two variables have changed.

quiz.q3.prompt.text: If a tool description is precise, does that authorize the model to execute any local function?

quiz.q3.a.text.text: Yes; the description itself is execution permission.

quiz.q3.a.feedback.text: A description only affects which call the model proposes. It grants no permission to execute.

quiz.q3.b.text.text: No; execution is still bound by the Python allowlist.

quiz.q3.b.feedback.text: Correct. The real scope of execution is decided by the program's allowlist. However well a description is written, it cannot get an unregistered function executed.

quiz.q3.explanation.text: Prompts and descriptions affect proposals. The program's allowlist decides the real scope of execution.

quiz.q4.prompt.text: What is the most direct risk of a misleading tool description?

quiz.q4.a.text.text: The model decides by the description but the code is what runs, so the result does not match the user's intent

quiz.q4.a.feedback.text: Correct. The "Misleading × Concatenate" cell in the matrix is exactly this case.

quiz.q4.b.text.text: The model refuses to call any tool

quiz.q4.b.feedback.text: Not necessarily. The model may still call, just in the wrong place.

quiz.q4.c.text.text: The runner raises an error and stops the run

quiz.q4.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The runner does not check whether a description is true, and a valid call runs as usual.

quiz.q4.explanation.text: The description is all the explanation the model can see. Only when it matches the code does the model's decision have a basis.

quiz.missing-input-screen.prompt.text: The rewrite's answer for "Failure boundary: missing addend" is "Please provide two numbers, such as 3 and 5." How will the screening judge it, and what should you do?

quiz.missing-input-screen.a.text.text: A hit, because it asks for numbers

quiz.missing-input-screen.a.feedback.text: Not quite. All three conditions must hold. This sentence contains the digits 3 and 5, so the "no digits in the whole text" condition fails.

quiz.missing-input-screen.b.text.text: A miss because it contains digits; read the original text to see that it is in fact asking

quiz.missing-input-screen.b.feedback.text: Correct. The screen recognizes only the literal text, so this is a misjudgment. The original text shows it really is asking for the missing numbers.

quiz.missing-input-screen.c.text.text: A miss, which means the variant's rule did not work

quiz.missing-input-screen.c.feedback.text: Not quite. A miss only means the literal text did not match. Reading the original shows the model asked, following the rule.

quiz.missing-input-screen.explanation.text: The screening rule is simple and easy to review, and also easy to misjudge. Whether it hits or misses, go back to the original text.

quiz.regression-next.prompt.text: In one pair of results, the baseline hit the screen and the variant missed. What should you do first?

quiz.regression-next.a.text.text: Read the variant's original text to see whether the new rule caused a side effect or the screen misjudged

quiz.regression-next.a.feedback.text: Correct. This is a clue of regression. Find out why before deciding whether to change anything.

quiz.regression-next.b.text.text: Switch straight back to the baseline, because the variant is certainly worse

quiz.regression-next.b.feedback.text: Not quite. One result could be sampling noise or a screening error.

quiz.regression-next.c.text.text: Ignore it, as long as most tasks got better

quiz.regression-next.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The report keeps regressions precisely so that something getting worse elsewhere is not quietly let through.

quiz.regression-next.explanation.text: For a regression, check the original text first and then repeat a few times. Do not conclude from one pair.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run the "Tool description: vague vs. clear" exercise and find the response where the model actually proposes a tool call instead of answering directly in text.

check-hunt.explanation.text: In that response, message.tool_calls has at least one item holding the function name and arguments. A response where tool_calls is empty or missing is just a text answer. This preset only records and screens the proposal and does not execute the tool. Which version of the tool description it appears under, you tell by comparing with the request of the same round.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's source, and tick each item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I can point to the one variable that changed between the two requests.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I checked that the two requests used the same model and sampling temperature.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I can explain why one pair cannot prove the variant is better in general.

check-points.item-4.text.text: I ran the tool description matrix and can point to the cell where the model's decision and the code's return do not line up.

code_notes.function.description.note.text: The usage-note field of the tool definition in the request; the two tool description presets change only this.

code_notes.description.note.text: That is, function.description; in the blank row the tool definition omits this field altogether.

code_notes.tool_spec.note.text: The function that builds the add_numbers tool definition; when passed None it omits the description field.
